product_scope: MyFitnessPal Meal Scan is a Premium/Premium+ mobile logging feature. It uses a live camera view, and in the newer iOS flow a gallery photo upload, to identify visible foods or ingredients in a meal. It proposes matching verified foods from MyFitnessPal's food database; the user confirms items, edits serving size or number of servings, searches for missed items, and adds the selections to the Diary. It is positioned as a logging-speed and adherence feature, not as a medical tool or a guaranteed measurement of calories. MyFitnessPal describes the recognition layer as machine learning plus computer vision trained on millions of images. Sources: https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/360045761612-Meal-Scan-FAQ ; https://blog.myfitnesspal.com/meal-scan/ ; https://www.passio.ai/blog/essential-guide-to-myfitnesspal-meal-scan
supported_platforms: Current public documentation says Meal Scan is available to Premium users on iOS 17 or newer and Android 12 or newer, with MyFitnessPal version 22.17 or newer and the device/app language set to English. Photo upload is documented as iOS-only and United States-only in the January 2026 FAQ. MyFitnessPal also has a web client and the app stores list iPhone/iPad/Apple Watch and Android clients, but the Meal Scan workflow itself is documented for mobile camera clients rather than the web. MyFitnessPal says third-party APK installations are unsupported. Sources: https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/360045761612-Meal-Scan-FAQ ; https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/4402625100941-Supported-Devices ; https://apps.apple.com/us/app/myfitnesspal-calorie-counter/id341232718 ; https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.myfitnesspal.android

recognition_behavior: The documented flow is: open the blue plus button, select Meal Scan, follow the capture guidance, and either hover the live camera over the food or use the shutter/upload-photo option. The recognizer can return multiple visible foods and suggested alternatives. The user selects the desired suggestion, adjusts serving size or number of servings, uses database search for anything missed, reviews the selections, and taps the checkmark and Add to Diary; items can be edited later from the Add Food page. MyFitnessPal and Passio say the system works best on common, clearly visible, separated ingredients. A peach viewed from the top can resemble an apple; hidden ingredients, mixed dishes, soups, smoothies, and foods obscured by other foods are expected failure cases. Sources: https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/360045761612-Meal-Scan-FAQ ; https://blog.myfitnesspal.com/meal-scan/ ; https://www.passio.ai/blog/essential-guide-to-myfitnesspal-meal-scan
identified_services: [uncertain] Passio AI/Nutrition-AI is explicitly named by MyFitnessPal as the partner behind the original 2020 Meal Scan and the 2025 enhanced feature, and Passio publishes a guide describing the MyFitnessPal integration. MyFitnessPal's January 2026 FAQ simultaneously says that the current Meal Scan uses models built and run by MyFitnessPal, trained on millions of images, and maps results to its own food database. Passio's public SDK exposes remote image recognition, food/nutrition lookup, and mobile SDKs; an older public Android analysis also contains Passio API/model URLs. The exact current division between MyFitnessPal-owned models, Passio SDK components, MyFitnessPal database services, and any cloud LLM is not disclosed. No public evidence found here proves a direct OpenAI or Google Gemini call from the MyFitnessPal app; model names mentioned in Passio's general platform documentation are not evidence of MyFitnessPal's configuration. local_inference_evidence: [uncertain] Evidence supporting on-device inference: the original 2020 MyFitnessPal launch describes real-time hover recognition and says the live Meal Scan function did not save or upload data from the phone camera; Passio launch material also described the feature as on-device real-time recognition. A public 2023 modified Android artifact contains a Passio food SDK, TFLiteRecognizer strings, a Passio Android-model download path, and a local visual-food database, which is consistent with the historical local mode. Evidence supporting cloud inference: the October 2025 enhancement added a photo-upload path, while Passio's current SDK documentation says modern photo logging is remote/cloud-side, uses recognizeImageRemote, requires connectivity, and treats bundled on-device models as legacy/not recommended. The most defensible conclusion is a versioned hybrid: the legacy live-camera path had local inference, while the later upload-photo path is likely remote; MyFitnessPal does not publish a current per-path trace, so this is not confirmed for every current build. Sources: https://blog.myfitnesspal.com/meal-scan/ ; https://passio.gitbook.io/nutrition-ai/mobile-sdks/mobile-sdk-overview ; https://passio.gitbook.io/nutrition-ai/fundamentals/developer-faq ; https://hybrid-analysis.com/sample/a90db24e60796fdb75f747ff91dd6f8c7bbeb115dbbd0cb03bbdbe7e28291d0e/654f4dd3a5d776830c0917c5
portion_and_nutrition_method: [uncertain] Public MyFitnessPal instructions establish food identification plus a database-backed serving workflow, not a documented end-to-end photo-to-grams method. The result appears to be a recognized food candidate mapped to a MyFitnessPal food entry, whose calories and nutrients are then read from the selected database serving; the user adjusts serving size and servings before logging. The 2020 Passio guide described automatic food amount estimation as a future capability, while current Passio SDK documentation says weight/volume estimates exist for certain foods, but MyFitnessPal's current Meal Scan FAQ does not say that automatic weight/volume estimation is exposed in Meal Scan. A single image also cannot reliably reveal cooking oil, recipe composition, hidden ingredients, or exact mass, so the product should be treated as an assisted database lookup with user correction rather than a measured nutrition result. Sources: https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/360045761612-Meal-Scan-FAQ ; https://www.passio.ai/blog/essential-guide-to-myfitnesspal-meal-scan ; https://passio.gitbook.io/nutrition-ai/mobile-sdks/mobile-sdk-overview ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38888538/

static_findings: The current public XAPK base APK has CAMERA and INTERNET permissions, Meal Scan-related Kotlin module/assets, MyFitnessPal food-database resources, and bundled ML Kit barcode models. No obvious food VLM/classifier model was present by standard model extensions in the XAPK tree. JADX was run against the base APK and produced a large decompiled source tree; the package is heavily obfuscated and shared-library code is present. The current static pass did not reveal a named Passio/OpenAI/Gemini food endpoint; provider attribution therefore comes from official product/vendor disclosures rather than this binary.
reverse_engineering_limits: No APK was installed or executed, no paid-account runtime session was captured, and no network trace was collected. Third-party public artifacts are untrusted inputs; model assets can be downloaded later, encrypted, or delivered in a split/native component. Static analysis cannot establish the current feature flag, image retention behavior, request payload, server-side model, data residency, or whether live-camera and gallery-upload paths use the same recognizer. MyFitnessPal's public pages also do not publish a model card or an independent Meal Scan accuracy benchmark.
candidate_models: For SuperNutrition rather than as a claim about MyFitnessPal's proprietary model: (1) EfficientNet-Lite or MobileNetV3, using an Apache-2.0-compatible TensorFlow distribution and fine-tuning on a controlled food taxonomy, is the best first local classifier for fast common-food recognition; it needs a separate detector/segmenter for multi-item plates. Source: https://blog.tensorflow.org/2020/03/higher-accuracy-on-vision-models-with-efficientnet-lite.html. (2) MobileCLIP/MobileCLIP2 S0-S2 provides image-text zero-shot retrieval and Apple reports roughly 3-15 ms and 50-150M parameters for the family, but Apple's released model weights are under a research-only Apple Machine Learning Research Model license, so they are not a safe commercial default. Sources: https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mobileclip ; https://github.com/apple/ml-mobileclip ; https://github.com/apple/ml-mobileclip/blob/main/LICENSE_MODELS. (3) SmolVLM-256M-Instruct is an Apache-2.0, image-plus-text 256M model intended for efficient multimodal inference and reported by its model card to run on one image with under 1GB of GPU RAM; use it for a prototype candidate generator or explanation layer, not as the authority for calories. Source: https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM-256M-Instruct. (4) Gemma 3n E2B/E4B is a commercially usable Google open-weight multimodal family optimized for phones, with visual/text input, a MobileNet-V5 vision encoder, selective parameter activation, and effective memory reduction; it is a higher-quality local fallback for capable devices but much heavier than a classifier and still needs food-specific validation. Sources: https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/gemma-3n ; https://deepmind.google/models/gemma/gemma-3n/. In all cases, use a canonical nutrition database after recognition instead of asking a generic VLM to invent calorie values.
mobile_runtime_support: Core ML is the native iOS route: it can convert models from PyTorch or TensorFlow and use CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine resources while keeping inference on-device. Google AI Edge/LiteRT supports custom model conversion and hardware-accelerated CPU/GPU/NPU deployment across Android and iOS; MediaPipe is useful for camera/task plumbing, and LiteRT-LM is the Google route for on-device multimodal language models. ONNX Runtime Mobile supports Android and iOS with CPU, XNNPACK, Android NNAPI, and iOS Core ML execution providers; its documentation recommends quantization and device-specific benchmarking. ExecuTorch supports exporting PyTorch models to Android and iOS with XNNPACK, Vulkan, Qualcomm QNN, Core ML, and MPS backends. Practical choice: LiteRT or ONNX Runtime for a compact detector/classifier; ExecuTorch or LiteRT-LM for a PyTorch/VLM experiment; Core ML for an iOS-specific optimized path. Sources: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coreml/ ; https://developers.google.com/edge ; https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/tutorials/mobile/ ; https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch/stable/pathway-quickstart.html
device_requirements: [uncertain] MyFitnessPal publishes only OS requirements, not RAM, accelerator, latency, or battery requirements for Meal Scan. Planning ranges for SuperNutrition should be treated as test targets: an INT8/FP16 food classifier/detector should fit in roughly 10-60 MB of model storage and target sub-100-200 ms per camera inference on recent phones; a local multimodal model needs substantially more memory and should be gated to devices with about 6-8 GB RAM until measured. Passio's SDK FAQ gives a useful historical anchor of roughly 40-60 MB for legacy on-device models, while its current remoteOnly mode downloads no models. Quantization reduces storage and bandwidth but can reduce fine-grained food discrimination; NPU/GPU acceleration lowers latency and battery cost but varies by chipset and unsupported operators can force CPU fallback. Benchmark on representative iOS 17 and Android 12+ devices with sustained camera use before setting a minimum. Sources: https://passio.gitbook.io/nutrition-ai/fundamentals/developer-faq ; https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/tutorials/mobile/ ; https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coreml/ ; https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch/stable/pathway-quickstart.html
expected_food_inference_quality: [uncertain] The strongest expected behavior is fast candidate generation for common, visually distinct, separated foods: MyFitnessPal says the feature can identify thousands of foods, and Passio recommends clear views, separated foods, and scanning ingredients before cooking. Likely weak cases are visually similar foods, low light or occlusion, mixed/blended dishes, sauces and oils, recipe-level composition, branded packaging without readable context, culturally varied foods, and portion size. The public materials provide no independent Meal Scan top-1/top-3 or calorie-error benchmark. General dietary-image research shows that portion and energy estimates require careful image protocols and can still overestimate energy, reinforcing the need for a user correction step. Treat recognition as a ranked suggestion with abstention, not ground truth; measure item accuracy, missed-item rate, serving-size error, calorie error against weighed meals, and calibration by food/cultural group. Sources: https://www.passio.ai/blog/essential-guide-to-myfitnesspal-meal-scan ; https://blog.myfitnesspal.com/meal-scan/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38888538/ ; https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/360045761612-Meal-Scan-FAQ
unit_cost_estimate: [uncertain] MyFitnessPal's negotiated provider cost is not public. As a Passio public-list-price proxy, the current platform page says one photo sent to the API consumes about 20,000-30,000 tokens. At the Pro refill price of $2.50 per 1M tokens, that is approximately $0.05-$0.075 per analyzed photo, or $0.10-$0.15 for two photos per meal, before the $2,999/month plan fee and any other application costs. At the Growth refill price of $10 per 1M tokens, the same photo is about $0.20-$0.30; Starter's $25 per 1M refill is about $0.50-$0.75. Included monthly tokens and fixed plan fees change the effective cost at lower volumes, and MFP may have a private enterprise rate. A local classifier has no per-photo API charge but consumes device storage, battery, engineering, model-update, and support budget. privacy_and_compliance: [uncertain] The original live-camera Meal Scan post says the function did not save or upload camera data, but that statement predates the 2025 gallery-photo upload path and should not be generalized to every current mode. MyFitnessPal's March 2025 privacy policy says it collects Food and Activity Diary Data such as foods, drinks, medications, calories, dietary restrictions, body measurements, conditions, progress photos, and notes; it treats diary data as potentially sensitive when it reveals or permits inference of a health condition. The policy also lists audio/electronic/visual information, says service providers may process information for hosting, storage, analytics, and other operations, and provides access, deletion, correction, and opt-out rights subject to law. The policy's retention rule is as long as necessary for stated purposes/legal requirements, with de-identified data potentially retained. Apple's App Store label says health/fitness, contact info, user content, identifiers, usage, and diagnostics may be linked to the user and that identifiers/usage may be used for tracking; Google Play says the app may share location, personal info, and device IDs, encrypts data in transit, and supports deletion requests. Passio's provider documentation says remote images are processed in the cloud and not stored under its standard setup, while on-device mode avoids transmitting photos; that does not prove MyFitnessPal's customer-side retention or subprocessor arrangement. For SuperNutrition, require explicit photo-processing consent, a no-training-on-user-images contract, short deletion windows, encryption, regional routing, a DPA/subprocessor list, user deletion/export, audit logs, and a clear offline-versus-cloud indicator. Sources: https://blog.myfitnesspal.com/meal-scan/ ; https://frontend.myfitnesspal.com/privacy-policy ; https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/34887736402445-How-do-we-retain-your-information ; https://support.myfitnesspal.com/hc/en-us/articles/34887671359885-How-does-MyFitnessPal-share-my-information ; https://apps.apple.com/us/app/myfitnesspal-calorie-counter/id341232718 ; https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.myfitnesspal.android ; https://passio.gitbook.io/nutrition-ai/fundamentals/developer-faq
recommendation: Use a transparent hybrid architecture as the next SuperNutrition experiment. Run a small, quantized local detector/classifier for common foods and visible components, keep the photo and first-pass embeddings on-device, map accepted candidates to a curated nutrition database, and require the user to confirm or adjust servings. Route only ambiguous, complex, or explicitly uploaded photos to a cloud recognizer such as a contracted Passio-style service; make the transfer opt-in, ephemeral, encrypted, region-aware, and visible in the UI. Do not copy MyFitnessPal's ambiguous provider story or infer exact calories from a generic VLM. First experiment: collect a consented, culturally diverse benchmark of roughly 300-500 meals with weighed portions and ingredient metadata; compare local-only, cloud-only, and hybrid modes for item accuracy, missed foods, serving-size error, calories/macros error, latency, battery, offline behavior, and privacy/retention. If evaluating Passio, obtain written answers on the exact SDK/model version, live versus upload routing, image retention, model training, data location, DPA, SLA, and price before production use.
